prize_parts.citation: for the theory and first experimental realisation of strong coupling between a single microwave photon and a superconducting artificial atom, establishing circuit quantum electrodynamics

statement.case_for: Circuit QED is the one candidate on this shortlist that most colleagues placed in their top four independently of field, which is a better sign than my own first place. It is a defined discovery with a defined date: the 2004 theory proposal and the two strong-coupling experiments showed that a single microwave photon in a resonator can be coupled coherently to an engineered artificial atom. The consequences are concrete: dispersive readout, resonator-mediated qubit coupling, the bus architecture, and quantum-limited amplification chains. Dozens of laboratories have reproduced and extended it for two decades, so maturity is not in question. The credit also splits cleanly into one theory name (Blais) and two experimental groups (Wallraff and Schoelkopf), which is rarer than it sounds on this list. Several colleagues who work far from the field (Mehlig, Lindroth, Olsson, Pearce) reached the same view on the merits, which weighs more with me than my own familiarity.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is sequencing. The 2025 prize recognised macroscopic quantum tunnelling and energy quantisation in an electric circuit, and a prize in the same platform one year later can look like a continuation. There is also a real attribution problem: Girvin and Huang are co-authors of the founding theory proposal, and the Yale group's other members and the transmon line sit close to the credited core. A three-name limit forces an allocation that someone will contest. Finally, one can fairly ask whether the discovery is an architecture rather than a finding about nature, and whether the committee would rather wait for a quantum-computing outcome.

responses.point: Danielsson ranks circuit QED only eighth, because of overlap with the 2025 circuit prize and because it may be enabling technology rather than a distinct discovery, and puts the experimental Higgs observation first.
responses.response: I take the overlap point seriously and cannot dismiss it. But the two are different physics: the 2025 work showed that a macroscopic circuit variable obeys quantum mechanics (tunnelling, level quantisation), whereas circuit QED showed coherent exchange between a single photon and an engineered atom, the framework for light-matter coupling that the earlier work did not supply. On the enabling-technology charge, strong coupling of one microwave photon to a solid-state atom was not obviously possible before 2004. It was a demonstration, and a surprise in how clean it was. I will concede that Higgs recognition is overdue in a way circuit QED is not, and that our disagreement is mainly about urgency. My difficulty with B005 is the four-name credit, which cannot be mapped onto the three-person limit without excluding someone with an equal claim.

responses.point: Kroll ranks optical lattice clocks first: a clear, original idea built on Katori's magic-wavelength scheme and Ye's record accuracy, with a clean two-laureate allocation, timely given the pending redefinition of the second.
responses.response: I agree that B031 has the cleanest attribution on the list and I have it third. My qualification is the one Kroll raises himself: the 2005 comb prize and the 2012 ion-control prize cover neighbouring ground, and a committee can reasonably ask whether lattice clocks are a new discovery or the best implementation of a prior one. The magic-wavelength idea is a genuine conceptual step, so I do not think it fails that test. Where I would not follow Kroll is on urgency. The redefinition of the second has not happened, and I would rather not tie the prize to a metrological decision still pending. I regard B031 as our best fallback if circuit QED is judged too close to 2025.

responses.point: Eriksson ranks magic-angle twisted bilayer graphene first, because a continuum-model flat-band prediction was followed by a decisive experiment and the platform is tunable and widely reproduced, while placing circuit QED fourth on account of its closeness to the 2025 prize.
responses.response: I share his admiration for the theory-then-experiment structure and ranked B024 second, so this is a disagreement of degree. My reservation is maturity of interpretation: the pairing mechanism of the superconductivity is unresolved, several correlated phases are still debated, and twist-angle disorder complicates the detailed phase diagrams. That makes B024 look early next to a topic where the physics is settled and used daily. I would also note that the credited experimental name, Jarillo-Herrero, stands for a team in which the first author is not credited, as Mehlig points out. On his 2025 worry we agree about the facts and differ in weight.

responses.point: Pearce ranks IceCube first as the opening of a new observational window, with the hard problem of background rejection solved, while ranking circuit QED second and warning against overlap with the previous circuit prize.
responses.response: I accept the instrumental achievement, and I have no competence to challenge his judgement of the detector and background problem. Detecting the diffuse flux in 2013 was a discovery in the strict sense. My hesitation is that the astrophysical origin of most of the flux is still open and the source evidence rests on few objects, which Danielsson also notes, so the discovery is mature but the science it opened is young. Credit among AMANDA and IceCube leaders is also less clean than for circuit QED. I appreciate that he ranks B016 second and shares the concern about overlap with 2025, so on this candidate I think his reservation and mine are the same.

responses.point: Olsson ranks aberration-corrected electron microscopy first as a decisive instrument invention, with a natural theory, realisation and application split among Rose, Haider and Urban, and regards the 2025 circuit prize as showing the committee's openness to the field rather than a barrier.
responses.response: Her reading of 2025 as evidence of openness is a fair counter to the sequencing worry, and I will use it. On B009 I agree about the attribution and the twenty years of use, but the question she raises herself, whether an electron microscopy prize meets the discovery-or-invention criterion in a physics sense after the Ruska precedent, is a real one. The STEM-corrector line outside the credited names also leaves open whether the TEM trio alone is a complete allocation. I rank it lower, and I would want the committee to settle the credit boundary before preferring it.

uncertainties: Whether the committee will read circuit QED as sufficiently distinct from the 2025 award, which I cannot settle from the supplied material and which I think is the deciding question.
Whether the exclusion of Girvin and Huang, co-authors of the founding theory proposal, and the Yale experimental group is defensible under a three-person limit.
Whether the prize should name the architecture (circuit QED) or wait for a quantum-computing outcome that may sharpen the credit.
Whether the allocation among Blais, Wallraff and Schoelkopf survives a closer check of the 2004 history than my memory allows.
statement.conflict_note: Specific connection to disclose: I direct the Wallenberg Centre for Quantum Technology at Chalmers, which builds superconducting quantum processors that rely on circuit QED, and I work in this field, with colleagues Per Delsing and C. M. Wilson at Chalmers, which also hosted researchers associated with the 2025 prize. The provided profile records no personal tie to Blais, Wallraff or Schoelkopf, but my institutional interest in B016 may warrant recusal or at least discounting of my support for it, and I have tried to weigh the alternatives with that in mind.
